title: five canon shell rules scope on bin/* with no extension constraint, so the shell critic claims non-shell files -- two are critical
body:
**FIVE CANON SHELL RULES SCOPE ON `bin/*` WITH NO EXTENSION CONSTRAINT, SO THE SHELL CRITIC CLAIMS EVERY FILE IN `bin/` WHATEVER LANGUAGE IT IS. TWO OF THE FIVE ARE `critical`.**

Reported from OUTSIDE this estate by lamplight-vc, re-driven here 2026-09-03 before filing.

## The measurement

    intent/plugins/claude/rules/shell/code/quote-expansions/RULE.md:23      severity: critical
    intent/plugins/claude/rules/shell/code/no-silent-exit-codes/RULE.md:22  severity: critical
    intent/plugins/claude/rules/shell/code/module-highlander/RULE.md:20     severity: warning
    intent/plugins/claude/rules/shell/code/set-euo-pipefail/RULE.md:22      severity: warning
    intent/plugins/claude/rules/shell/code/no-parse-ls/RULE.md:22           severity: warning

Each carries the same `applies_to` block:

    applies_to:
      - "**/*.sh"
      - "**/*.bash"
      - "bin/*"

**The first two patterns are extension-constrained and correct. The third is not.** `bin/*` matches every entry in `bin/` regardless of what it is: a Python script, a Lua file, a compiled binary, a symlink, a data file.

## Why the third pattern is there at all, and why removing it is not the fix

It is there because the convention it serves is real: **an executable shell script in `bin/` usually carries no extension.** `bin/intent` is exactly that. So deleting the pattern would silently drop the estate's own scripts out of scope of five rules including two critical ones -- **which is the opposite failure and is quieter.**

**The pattern encodes "a shell script without an extension" and expresses it as "anything in `bin/`".** That is a proxy standing in for a property it cannot see, which is this estate's most-instanced defect class: the instrument measures a LOCATION and the rule claims a LANGUAGE.

## Blast radius

These are CANON rules, served from the install to every consuming estate. **An estate whose `bin/` holds anything that is not shell gets critical findings against files in a language the rules do not describe.** This estate does not feel it, because its `bin/` is shell.

## Not claimed

The remedy. Candidates: a shebang check at match time; an explicit exclusion list; a `applies_to_shebang:` field alongside `applies_to:`; or scoping to `bin/*` only where the critic can confirm the file is shell. **Whichever is chosen has to keep extension-less shell scripts IN scope**, which is the constraint that makes the naive fix wrong. Also not claimed: how many estates currently carry non-shell files in `bin/`; nobody has counted.


---

## DRIVEN ON v3.0.0 2026-09-05, AND `bin/*` DOES NOT LACK AN EXTENSION CONSTRAINT -- IT OVERRIDES ONE

This row is written as *the third pattern is not extension-constrained*, which reads as an omission. **It is stronger than that: `bin/*` claims a file that names its own language.**

Driven against the published binary (`80d8b2ca`) with the tag's own rule pack, three arms:

| file | bytes | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bin/luatool` | a Lua script whose line 2 is the comment `-- shells out for the legacy path: cat $1 \| grep x` | **`[CRITICAL] IN-SH-CODE-001 at bin/luatool:2`** |
| `src/luatool.lua` | **identical** | `ok: no shell findings` |
| `bin/luatool.lua` | **identical** | **`[CRITICAL] IN-SH-CODE-001 at bin/luatool.lua:2`** |

Arm 2 establishes that the discriminator is the PATH and not the content. **Arm 3 is the new part: `.lua` is present, unambiguous, and loses to `bin/*`.** The critic flags a comment in a Lua file for being unquoted shell.

So a remedy shaped as *add an extension constraint* is not enough on its own -- an estate whose non-shell files in `bin/` already carry extensions is not helped by it. The pattern has to stop claiming a file whose language is otherwise determinable, whichever way that is determined.

### One correction to this row's own framing

The five rules are real and their `applies_to` is as quoted, but **only two of the six shell rules ARM on this build** (`critic: shell -- 2 of 6 rule(s) ASKED; 4 declared unanswerable`). So the live exposure is narrower than five rules at the moment, and the two that arm include `IN-SH-CODE-001`, which is one of the two `critical` ones. **The unarmed four become live exposure the day their proxies are answerable**, so the row's severity is about what the scoping WILL do, not only what it does today.

### A note on the instrument, which is the reusable part

The first run of this probe reported four clean arms. **All four were worthless** -- the rules tree was not in the install, and the critic said so in its own output on every one of them: `0 armed in total`. The verdict line and the denominator line disagreed, and only the denominator was true. **An instrument that volunteers its own denominator is what catches a rig error the operator cannot see**, and the four greens would otherwise have gone into this issue as evidence.
